posts.title: CAP Theorem: Pick Two, Whether You Like It or Not
posts.subtitle: Why every distributed database is secretly a CP system or an AP system
posts.summary: CAP theorem says a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. Since partitions aren't optional in real networks, the real design choice is CP vs. AP during a partition — and PACELC extends the idea to cover the latency/consistency tradeoff that exists even when nothing is broken.

slides.title: Pick Two: The Theorem Every Distributed Database Obeys
slides.body: CAP theorem, formalized by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch in 2002 from Eric Brewer's 2000 conjecture, says a distributed data store can't simultaneously guarantee Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance — at most two of three, whenever the network is behaving badly.
bullets: C = every read gets the latest write, or an error — this is linearizability
A = every request to a working node gets a non-error response
P = the system keeps working even when nodes can't talk to each other

slides.title: Networks Partition. That's Not Optional.
slides.body: The theorem is often mistaught as 'pick any 2 of 3,' but partition tolerance isn't really a choice in a real distributed system — network links fail, packets drop, and nodes go dark. The actual decision you're making is: what happens to the other two properties during a partition?
bullets: A single-node database can be perfectly consistent and available — it has no partition to worry about
The moment you replicate data across machines or regions, partitions become a when, not an if
So CAP in practice is really 'CP vs AP': when a partition hits, do you sacrifice consistency or availability?

slides.title: CP or AP: The Real Fork in the Road
slides.body: During a network partition, a CP system refuses to answer (or returns an error) rather than risk serving stale data; an AP system keeps answering with whatever data it has locally, even if it might be out of date.
bullets: CP example: a leader-based system like etcd or ZooKeeper stops accepting writes on the minority side of a partition rather than risk divergence
AP example: Cassandra or DynamoDB keep serving reads and writes on both sides of a partition, then reconcile once it heals
Neither choice is 'wrong' — it depends on whether stale data or downtime is more costly for that specific system

slides.title: Worked Example: A Bank vs. A Shopping Cart
slides.body: A funds-transfer ledger and a shopping cart make opposite CAP choices for good reason.
bullets: Funds transfer (CP-leaning): better to reject a transaction during a partition than risk two nodes both approving a double-spend — Google Spanner uses synchronized atomic clocks (TrueTime) plus a private global network to get strong consistency with very high, not theoretically perfect, availability

Shopping cart (AP-leaning): better to let a customer add an item during a partition, even if two replicas briefly disagree, than show them an error and lose the sale — Amazon's original Dynamo design explicitly chose availability over strict consistency for the cart
Same theorem, opposite real-world answer, because the cost of 'wrong' data differs

slides.title: CP vs AP Systems, By Example
slides.body: 'Spanner beats CAP' is a common myth — it doesn't violate the theorem, it just engineers partitions to be so rare that the CP tradeoff barely shows up in practice.

rows: Both sides keep serving, reconcile later
Writes need a majority; minority side degrades to read-only
TrueTime + private network make partitions extremely rare

slides.title: CAP's Blind Spot: What Happens With No Partition?
slides.body: CAP only describes behavior during a partition, but distributed systems spend almost all their time not partitioned, and there's still a tradeoff during normal operation. Daniel Abadi's 2010 PACELC extension names it directly.
bullets: PACELC: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency (that's CAP) — Else, choose Latency or Consistency
Even with a healthy network, waiting for every replica to confirm a write (strong consistency) adds latency that a single-region read wouldn't have
This is why systems like DynamoDB let you choose 'eventually consistent' vs 'strongly consistent' reads per request — you're picking a point on the latency/consistency line, not just the CAP triangle

slides.title: Where CAP Gets Misused
slides.body: CAP is a theorem about one specific guarantee (linearizable consistency) under one specific failure mode (total network partition) — using it to justify every architecture decision overstates what it actually proves.
bullets: CAP says nothing about latency, throughput, or partial/regional failures — those need PACELC or empirical testing, not CAP alone
'Eventual consistency' isn't one thing — different AP systems give very different staleness guarantees, so 'we're AP' doesn't tell you much on its own

Don't default to CP everywhere: most reads in most apps (profile pages, product listings) tolerate slightly stale data just fine, and paying the availability/latency cost for linearizability there is often wasted

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: CAP theorem: pick at most 2 of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance — but partition tolerance isn't optional for a real distributed system, so the real choice is CP vs AP during a partition
CP systems (etcd, ZooKeeper, Spanner) refuse or degrade during a partition to protect consistency; AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB default) keep answering and reconcile later
Google Spanner doesn't break CAP — it engineers partitions to be rare enough that the CP cost is barely noticeable
PACELC fills CAP's gap: even without a partition, every request still trades latency against consistency

questions.prompt: In CAP theorem, what does "Consistency" specifically mean?
options: Every node runs the same code version
Every read receives the most recent write, or an error (linearizability)
The database schema never changes
All nodes respond within the same time limit
questions.explanation: CAP's "C" specifically means linearizability: a read must return the most recent write or an error, not just "the same value on every node eventually."

questions.prompt: Why is "pick any 2 of 3" a misleading way to describe CAP in practice?
options: Because all three properties are always achievable together
Because partition tolerance isn't really optional for a real distributed system — the actual choice is what happens to C or A during a partition
Because CAP only applies to single-node databases
Because availability and consistency mean the same thing
questions.explanation: Real networks partition regardless of what you'd prefer, so a distributed system can't actually choose to drop P — the meaningful design decision is whether it favors C or A once a partition happens.

questions.prompt: What gap in CAP theorem does PACELC address?
options: It clarifies that partitions never actually happen in real networks
It describes a latency-vs-consistency tradeoff that exists even when there's no partition
It replaces "Availability" with "Authentication"
It proves CAP theorem is wrong
questions.explanation: PACELC extends CAP by pointing out that even during normal operation (no partition), a system still trades latency against consistency — a tradeoff CAP is silent on.
